title: Y-R-H
hookLine: Torah is linked to yarah: to aim, to point, to teach

cards: A stranger on the sidewalk, phone dead, clearly lost, asks how to get to the train. Nobody hands over a rulebook. You lift an arm and point.
That way, past the bakery, then left. The whole answer is in the arm: a direction, aimed. Hold that picture next to a word often translated as law.
Torah. Jewish tradition links it to a root that has nothing to do with courtrooms. Yud, resh, heh: Y-R-H.

teach.b: Turn yarah four ways. First, shooting. Jonathan, King Saul's son, needs to warn his friend David without being seen.
He goes out to a field with a boy and a bow: "Run, find now the arrows which I shoot." Where the arrows land is the message. Shoot is from this root; an arrow is aim made visible.
When Jacob's family goes down to Egypt, Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph "to show the way before him unto Goshen." To show the way, l'horot, again Y-R-H. Not carrying anyone.
Pointing. Third, teaching. A teacher is a moreh, the one who points.

teach.h: TEACH: THE TEACHING OF THY MOTHER.
teach.b: In Proverbs a parent says, "Hear, my son, the instruction of thy father, And forsake not the teaching of thy mother." The teaching of thy mother: torat imecha, a phrase you met on day one thousand forty-two.
The old Jewish Publication Society translation renders torah there not as law, but as teaching. Fourth, the Torah itself. English often calls it the Law, and it does contain law.

teach.h: TORAH: A TEACHING THAT AIMS YOU.
teach.b: But, as you first heard on day twenty, tradition hears this root underneath: a teaching that aims you and sends you out, like Jonathan's arrow or Judah on the road to Goshen.
Not a fence around you. An arm lifted, saying: that way. Open a Torah scroll, by this reading, and you're asking for directions.

how: Jews read the Torah aloud in synagogue and study it with commentaries; in Hebrew a teacher is a moreh, from the root that tradition links to the word Torah.

o: a root meaning to see, as in God will provide
a root meaning to shoot or point, and so to teach
a root meaning to fear, as in fear of heaven

p: run, find the arrows I shoot

s: the word torah only ever means law
Proverbs uses it for a mother's teaching: forsake not the teaching of thy mother.
the root Y-R-H can mean to shoot an arrow
Jonathan uses it in the field: the arrows which I shoot.
Judah was sent ahead to carry Jacob to Goshen
he was sent to show the way: to point it.

games.q: you're Jonathan. you have to warn your friend David, who is hiding in a field, without anyone noticing. how do you send the message?
games.why: he shoots arrows and calls to the boy fetching them; where they fall is the message for David.

practice: Let the week ahead come into view and pick one thing worth aiming at, small and real: finish a letter, visit someone, learn one more line.
Picture it as a target a little way off, and then the arrow leaving the bow, the very first step you'd take toward it. Hold your aim steady, and if you pray, bring the goal into the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Y-R-H. Yud, resh, heh: yarah, to shoot, to point, to teach; moreh, a teacher; and, tradition says, Torah, a teaching that aims. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: teaching, instruction; linked by tradition to yarah, to aim.

carryVoice: Your line: torah means aiming. A mother's torah is the way she points her child. I'll be here tomorrow.
